title: Principles of Marketing

pattern.summary: 8 questions, attempt any 5, each carries 20 marks. All theory. Q8 is always 'short notes on any four of six'. Questions repeat heavily — use Indian brand examples (Amul, Maggi, Tata, Patanjali) in every answer.

choosing: Promotion mix, distribution channels, marketing environment, product life cycle and segmentation/targeting come up in almost every paper — five dependable choices.
Q8 (four notes out of six) rewards broad revision: digital, green, social and rural marketing, branding and services recur.

topics.name: Promotion Mix & IMC
topics.summary: Role of promotion, components of the promotion mix, choosing the best tool, integrated marketing communication.
points: Promotion: communicating with customers to inform, persuade and remind them about a product.

Components: advertising (paid, non-personal, mass reach — costly, one-way), personal selling (face-to-face, flexible — expensive per contact), sales promotion (short-term incentives: coupons, discounts, contests — quick sales, can hurt brand), publicity/PR (unpaid media coverage — credible, not controllable), direct marketing (catalogues, e-mail, telemarketing — targeted, measurable).
Factors in choosing the mix: nature of product (consumer vs industrial), stage of PLC, target market size and spread, push vs pull strategy, budget, competition.
Integrated marketing communication: coordinating all promotion tools to deliver one consistent message.
Criticism of advertising: raises prices, misleading claims, promotes materialism, creates unnecessary wants.
Selling theories: AIDA, right set of circumstances, buying formula, behavioural equation.
Communication process: sender → encoding → message → media → decoding → receiver → response → feedback, with noise in between.
Advertising media decisions: choosing the media type (press, TV, radio, outdoor, internet) and vehicle by reach, frequency, cost and fit with the audience.
topics.frame: Meaning → each component with merits and limits (a table works well) → selection factors → Indian example → conclusion.

topics.name: Channels of Distribution
topics.summary: Types of channels, functions of channel members and middlemen, factors in channel choice, intensity of distribution, wholesalers.
points: Channel of distribution: route through which goods pass from producer to consumer.
Types: zero-level (direct — Amway, company websites), one-level (producer → retailer → consumer), two-level (producer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer), three-level (with agents).
Functions: information, promotion, contact, matching (sorting, grading, packaging), negotiation, physical distribution, financing, risk-taking.
Role of middlemen: reduce the number of transactions, provide assortment, storage, credit, market feedback.

Factors in channel choice: product (perishability, value, technical nature), market (number and location of buyers, order size), company (resources, control desired), middlemen (availability, cost), environment and competition.
Intensity: intensive (convenience goods everywhere — soap), selective (few outlets — electronics), exclusive (one dealer per area — luxury cars).
Services of wholesalers: to manufacturers (bulk buying, storage, finance, market information) and to retailers (assortment, credit, quick supply).
Types of middlemen: merchant middlemen (wholesalers, retailers — take title) and agent middlemen (brokers, commission agents — do not).
Physical distribution moves goods to customers at the right time and place at least total cost. Tasks: order processing, warehousing, inventory control, transportation and information monitoring.
topics.frame: Meaning → channel diagram (levels) → functions or factors as headed points → examples → conclusion.
mistakes: Skipping the channel-level diagram — a simple flow chart earns marks.

topics.name: Marketing Environment
topics.summary: Meaning, importance of environmental scanning, micro and macro environment.
points: Marketing environment: all forces outside marketing management that affect its ability to build customer relationships.
Why scan: spot opportunities and threats, plan strategy, adapt to change, beat competitors.
Micro environment (close to the company): company's internal departments, suppliers, marketing intermediaries, customers, competitors, publics.
Macro environment (PESTLE-type forces): demographic, economic, natural/ecological, technological, political-legal, socio-cultural.
Examples: rising incomes and smartphones (economic, technological) driving e-commerce; GST (legal) changing pricing; health awareness (cultural) boosting organic foods.
Government regulations affecting marketing in India include the Competition Act, the Consumer Protection Act, the Essential Commodities Act and laws on weights, measures and advertising.
topics.frame: Meaning → micro and macro forces in two groups, one Indian example each → importance of scanning → conclusion.

topics.name: Segmentation, Targeting & Positioning
topics.summary: Bases of consumer market segmentation, segmentation vs targeting, targeting strategies, positioning.
points: Segmentation: dividing a market into groups of buyers with similar needs.

Bases: geographic (region, urban/rural, climate), demographic (age, gender, income, occupation, family size), psychographic (lifestyle, personality, values), behavioural (occasion, benefits sought, usage rate, loyalty).
Segmentation divides the market; targeting chooses which segments to serve.

Targeting strategies: undifferentiated/mass (one offer for all), differentiated (different offers for several segments — Maruti's range), concentrated/niche (one segment — Rolex), micro-marketing (local or individual).
Positioning: creating a distinct place for the brand in the customer's mind — by attribute, benefit, price-quality, use, user, competitor (e.g. Volvo = safety).
Requirements of effective segments: measurable, accessible, substantial, differentiable, actionable.
topics.frame: Meaning → bases or strategies as headed points with brand examples → conclusion.

topics.name: Product Life Cycle
topics.summary: Stages of the PLC and marketing strategies at each stage.
points: PLC: stages a product passes through in the market — introduction, growth, maturity, decline.
Introduction: low sales, high costs, losses; strategy — create awareness, trial offers, skimming or penetration pricing, limited distribution.
Growth: sales rise fast, competitors enter, profits rise; strategy — improve quality, add features, enter new segments, widen distribution, brand-preference advertising.
Maturity: sales peak and slow, intense competition; strategy — modify market, product and marketing mix, price cuts, promotions.
Decline: sales and profits fall; strategy — cut costs, harvest, reposition or withdraw.
Examples: feature phones (decline), electric vehicles (growth), toothpaste (maturity).
topics.frame: Meaning → PLC curve diagram (sales and profit vs time) → each stage: features + strategy → conclusion.

topics.name: Pricing
topics.summary: Relevance and objectives of pricing, factors affecting price, pricing methods, geographical pricing, break-even.
points: Price is the only element of the marketing mix that brings revenue; it signals quality and affects demand.
Objectives: profit maximisation, target return, market share, survival, market skimming, penetration, meeting competition, product-quality leadership.
Factors: internal (costs, objectives, marketing mix, product life-cycle stage) and external (demand, competition, government regulation, economic conditions, buyers' perception).
Methods: cost-based (cost-plus, mark-up, break-even/target profit), demand-based (perceived value, price discrimination), competition-based (going-rate, sealed bid).
Geographical pricing: FOB origin, uniform delivered, zone pricing, basing-point, freight absorption.
Break-even point = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit).
International price quotations: EXW, FOB, CIF and other Incoterms.
Discounts and allowances off the list price: quantity, trade, cash and seasonal discounts, and promotional allowances.
Pricing a new product: market skimming (high price first, lowered later) or market penetration (low price to win a large share quickly). Also fixed vs flexible price policy and unit pricing.

Price regulation in India: Competition Act, 2002 (resale price maintenance, price discrimination, collective price fixing, predatory pricing, bargain and deceptive pricing, unreasonably high prices), Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (excessive and deceptive pricing), Essential Commodities Act 1955, Drugs (Price Control) Order 2013, IDR Act 1951 and Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules 2011.
topics.frame: Meaning → objectives or methods as headed points with examples → conclusion.

topics.name: Services Marketing
topics.summary: Goods vs services, characteristics of services, challenges in marketing services.
points: Service: an intangible activity offered for sale (banking, hotels, education).
Characteristics: intangibility, inseparability (produced and consumed together), variability/heterogeneity, perishability, no ownership.
Goods vs services: tangible vs intangible, can be stored vs perishable, standardised vs variable, ownership transfers vs does not.
Challenges: showing quality before purchase, keeping service consistent, matching supply with fluctuating demand, pricing intangibles, training staff, managing customer participation.
Extended mix (7 Ps): product, price, place, promotion + people, process, physical evidence.
topics.frame: Meaning → characteristics with examples → challenges → 7 Ps → conclusion.

topics.name: Consumer Behaviour & Buying Process
topics.summary: Factors influencing consumer behaviour and the stages of the buying decision (e.g. buying a washing machine or TV).
points: Factors: cultural (culture, sub-culture, social class), social (reference groups, family, roles and status), personal (age, life-cycle stage, occupation, income, lifestyle, personality), psychological (motivation, perception, learning, beliefs and attitudes).
Buying decision process: need recognition → information search → evaluation of alternatives → purchase decision → post-purchase behaviour.

Example (washing machine): the old one breaks (need) → asks friends, reads reviews, visits stores (search) → compares capacity, brand, price, warranty (evaluation) → buys a front-load model during a sale (purchase) → satisfaction or cognitive dissonance (post-purchase).
Buyer vs user: the person who buys may not be the one who uses the product; marketers must reach both.
topics.frame: Meaning → five stages as a flow chart applied to the product in the question → factors → conclusion.
mistakes: Describing stages without applying them to the product the question names.

topics.name: New Product Development
points: New product: original, improved or modified product, or a new brand.
Steps: idea generation → idea screening → concept development and testing → marketing strategy → business analysis → product development → test marketing → commercialisation.
Why it is complex: high cost, high failure rate, long time, changing customer needs, competition.
Example: Maggi Oats Noodles or a new flavour — screened, test-marketed in a few cities before national launch.
New products fail because of poor market research, weak product, wrong timing or price, weak promotion, or strong competition.
topics.frame: Meaning → steps as a numbered flow chart with one line each → example → conclusion.

topics.name: Digital, Green, Social & Other New Marketing
topics.summary: Digital marketing and its tools, e-retailing, green, social, relationship, experiential and direct marketing.
points: Digital marketing: promoting through digital channels. Tools: SEO, SEM/pay-per-click, social media, content, e-mail, affiliate and influencer marketing, mobile apps. Advantages: low cost, targeting, measurable, two-way. Limits: clutter, privacy concerns, needs skills, digital divide.
E-retailing: selling to consumers online (Amazon, Flipkart).
Green marketing: promoting environmentally safe products and practices (eco-labels, recyclable packaging).
Social marketing: using marketing to promote social good (Swachh Bharat, anti-smoking).
Relationship marketing: building long-term customer relationships (loyalty programmes, CRM).
Experiential marketing: engaging customers through memorable brand experiences (product trials, pop-up events).
Consumerism (from the 1960s): the movement to protect consumers' rights against unfair business practices.
Other new approaches in the book: face-to-face, internal (marketing to one's own employees), location-based, and augmented and virtual reality marketing.
topics.frame: Meaning → features or tools as headed points → Indian example → merits and limits → conclusion.

topics.name: Product Classification, Packaging & Branding
topics.summary: Classification of products, product mix, packaging functions and strategies, branding.
points: Consumer products: convenience, shopping, speciality, unsought. Industrial products: materials and parts, capital items, supplies and services. Also durable vs non-durable.
Product mix: all product lines a company sells — width, length, depth, consistency.
Packaging functions: protection, convenience, information, promotion ('silent salesman'), identification.
Packaging strategies: family packaging, reusable packaging, multiple packaging, kit packaging, changing the package.
Branding: name, term, sign or design that identifies a seller's product. Benefits: recognition, loyalty, premium pricing, easier new launches. Types: individual, family, private (store) brands.
Product-mix strategies: expanding or contracting the mix, stretching a line up or down, and product diversification into new lines.
topics.frame: Meaning → classification chart or functions as headed points → examples → conclusion.

topics.name: Rural Marketing
topics.summary: Meaning, features and challenges of rural markets, 4 A's of rural marketing.
points: Rural marketing: marketing goods and services to rural consumers (and rural produce to urban markets).
Features: large and scattered population, agriculture-dependent income, low literacy, seasonal demand, strong traditions, growing incomes and aspirations.
Challenges: poor roads and storage, low and irregular incomes, communication barriers, many languages, spurious products, credit needs.
4 A's: availability (reach every village), affordability (small packs — sachets), acceptability (products suited to rural needs), awareness (vernacular media, haats, melas).
Examples: HUL's Project Shakti, ITC e-Choupal, sachet shampoos.
topics.frame: Meaning → features/challenges → 4 A's with examples → conclusion.

topics.name: Marketing Concept & Marketing Mix
topics.summary: Marketing vs selling, relevance of marketing, the 4 Ps.
points: Marketing: identifying and satisfying customer needs profitably.
Marketing vs selling: customer needs vs seller's need to sell; long term vs short term; integrated marketing vs sales push.
Marketing mix (4 Ps): product, price, place, promotion — extended to 7 Ps for services.
Relevance: creates demand, satisfies customers, builds brands, generates revenue and employment, raises living standards.
Marketing concepts evolved in stages: production → product → selling → marketing → societal marketing.
topics.frame: Meaning → comparison table (marketing vs selling) → 4 Ps with one example each → conclusion.
